assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock combines the magic-wavelength idea with spectroscopy of ultranarrow forbidden transitions in trapped neutral atoms. It brings a very large number of atoms into a Lamb-Dicke regime, so quantum projection noise and Doppler/recoil shifts are controlled at the same time. It is a genuine conceptual step, not an incremental improvement. It has delivered fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, tests of relativistic time dilation over centimetre height differences, and constraints on drifting constants. These are the kinds of precision tests that tell us something about nature, and the field is close to my own.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice scheme (2001-2003) and made early demonstrations. Ye's group drove the strontium clocks to record accuracy and carried out the comparisons and gravitational-redshift tests. Together they cover the invention and the realisation. Other contributors exist (for example Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow and others), so a three-person limit leaves some contributions out, but the two-person configuration is clear and defensible.
assessment.maturity: Many independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE, NIST and others) have reproduced and extended the clocks, with mutual agreement at the 1e-18 level. The interpretation is stable and the work is ripe. The redefinition of the SI second is being prepared, so recognition would be timely.
uncertainties: Whether the Committee would see this as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 optical comb and 2012 trapped-ion prizes is a judgement call.
Allocation relative to other early contributors, for example Lemonde or Ludlow, is not settled by the supplied credit.
I have not independently verified the exact priority dates and record uncertainty values.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realise Hubbard models with tunable parameters. The superfluid to Mott insulator transition, fermionic Hubbard physics, and single-site-resolved quantum gas microscopy let us look directly at correlated many-body states. This is a fundamental change in how many-body quantum mechanics can be studied, since we can measure what a solid-state sample hides. The results are clear, quantitative and have been used widely.
assessment.attribution: Greiner and Bloch performed the 2002 Mott transition experiment; Bloch and Greiner developed the quantum gas microscope, and Esslinger led the fermionic Hubbard and band-insulator work. Zoller (with Jaksch et al.) provided the theoretical proposal, but Jaksch is not in the supplied credited names; Zoller is listed in other entries. Choosing Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger gives a reasonable experimental triple, though Greiner's relative role versus Bloch (his former collaborator) and other microscope groups (Greiner, Bakr, Gross, Kuhr) is partly unresolved.
assessment.maturity: Highly mature: many groups have reproduced the main results over more than two decades, and simulation of Hubbard physics is now routine. The open question is whether the most important quantitative result (for example the antiferromagnetic or d-wave regime) has been reached, and some may say the field's best outcome is still ahead.
uncertainties: The strict boundary between this entry and the controlled-atom quantum information entry is not clean; a joint recognition could be considered.
Theory credit (Zoller, Jaksch) falls outside the three experimentalists chosen.
I have not verified microscope priority among several groups.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The experimental discovery of the Higgs boson in 2012 confirmed the mechanism of electroweak symmetry breaking predicted decades earlier and completed the Standard Model's particle content. It is a milestone of experimental physics of the highest clarity, and it was the central goal of the LHC. I defer to my particle-physics colleagues for the finer points, but the significance is plain.
assessment.attribution: The 2013 prize recognised theory. For the experiments, credit is spread over thousands of people in two collaborations. Spokespersons and project founders (Gianotti, Jenni for ATLAS; Della Negra, Virdee for CMS) are the natural proxies, but the four supplied names exceed the three-laureate limit, and any three excludes one of them. Fairness between the collaborations is unresolved and the rules of the prize make this very hard.
assessment.maturity: Very mature: two independent experiments, extensive coupling measurements, and a stable interpretation. Timing is by now almost overdue, and the allocation difficulty is the main obstacle.
uncertainties: Whether a person-based award can fairly represent two large collaborations.
The choice of three of four credited names is arbitrary to a degree; Tejinder Virdee is equally defensible and the balance between ATLAS and CMS is a judgement.
I defer on the relative weight of contributions to my particle-physics colleagues.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cirac and Zoller proposed the trapped-ion quantum gate and a framework for quantum simulation with controlled atoms, and Blatt's group carried out entangling operations, quantum simulation and error-correction demonstrations with ions. The idea of using well-controlled atoms as quantum computers and simulators changed AMO physics and links to the quantum-limit theme. Parts are already covered by the 2012 Wineland prize (control of individual quantum systems), and the 2022 prize on entanglement.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller are the clear theoretical originators of the ion gate proposal. Blatt is a leading experimentalist, but Wineland already holds a prize for the gate foundations and Monroe, Kielpinski and others also did decisive early work. Bloch is credited here but I assign him to the optical lattice entry, so the pairing is a compromise.
assessment.maturity: Experimental demonstrations are reproduced across many groups, but the full promise of quantum computing is still maturing. The scientific idea is established, though some parts overlap with earlier prizes and the technology may yet reshape what deserves recognition.
uncertainties: Overlap with 2012 and 2022 prizes.
Choice of experimental representative (Blatt versus Monroe, Wineland or others outside the credited names).
Compound candidate whose parts (gates, simulation, error correction) could need separate recognition.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators opened a new class of matter defined by topology and spin-orbit coupling. Kane and Mele's theory showed that spin-orbit coupling in graphene could give a topological state, and the Z2 classification followed. Molenkamp's group observed the effect in HgTe quantum wells, following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal. It is an elegant, unexpected idea with experimental confirmation.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele are the central theorists; Molenkamp is the experimental discoverer. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang (HgTe proposal), Fu, Moore, Balents and Hasan (3D topological insulators) also made decisive contributions, and these are not within the supplied names for this entry. A three-person split will leave out important people, and this is the main weakness.
assessment.maturity: Mature: many experiments, a large literature and a stable theoretical framework. Still, the transport quantisation in HgTe is modest and the 2016 prize already honoured topological phases of matter.
uncertainties: Strong overlap with the 2016 topological-phase prize.
Credit for Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and the 3D case is outside the supplied names.
I defer to colleagues in condensed matter on the relative priority.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: IceCube's detection of a diffuse flux of astrophysical neutrinos and the association with the blazar TXS 0506+056 opened a new window on the high-energy universe. It is a discovery that nature supplied something nobody could predict in detail, and a large detector (a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice) was a bold experimental conception.
assessment.attribution: Halzen conceived and led IceCube; Karle and Spiering contributed to the design, the analysis and the earlier AMANDA and other efforts. Credit is shared in a collaboration of hundreds, and other leaders (for example the Baikal and ANTARES pioneers, and the earlier DUMAND people) have claims.
assessment.maturity: The diffuse flux is well established, but source identification is limited to a few associations, and the origin of the flux is largely unsolved. Recognition may be somewhat early.
uncertainties: Source identification remains thin.
Allocation among IceCube leaders and predecessor projects.
I defer to astrophysics colleagues on maturity.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg blockade gives controllable strong interactions between neutral atoms, and tweezer arrays now allow programmable many-body quantum simulation and gate operations. It combines simple atomic physics (which I know well) with new applications in quantum simulation, with surprising results such as quantum scars and new phases. The field is fast moving and rich.
assessment.attribution: Lukin, Browaeys and Saffman are credited; Jaksch, Lukin and Zoller made the blockade proposal (2000-2001), and Weiss, Regal, Bernien, Endres and Greiner's tweezer groups also are important. The credited names do not include all decisive contributors, and Zoller and Jaksch are missing in this entry.
assessment.maturity: Confirmation is strong across several laboratories, but the field is young, and the most important results are recent, so I consider the recognition early compared to others on my list.
uncertainties: Premature relative to similar atomic-physics candidates.
Missing credit for proposal and tweezer-array pioneers.
Whether the scientific discovery is the blockade or the programmable platform is not clear.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Aharonov-Bohm effect and Berry's geometric phase show that phase is physically meaningful in quantum mechanics, and they are among the concepts that connect quantum mechanics to topology. These are clear, fundamental ideas that appear in atomic, molecular and condensed matter physics, a point which I appreciate very much from my own field.
assessment.attribution: Aharonov and Bohm (1959) first described the effect, and Bohm is deceased and cannot be credited; Berry's 1984 phase is clearly his. Ehrenberg and Siday made earlier related contributions, and Pancharatnam an earlier optical version. This history complicates a fair pairing.
assessment.maturity: The effects are verified in many experiments (Tonomura's electron holography, interferometry and molecular physics), so confirmation is complete. Recognition is, if anything, long overdue, which raises questions of timing and of the committee's preference for discoveries rather than concepts.
uncertainties: Priority history (Ehrenberg-Siday, Pancharatnam) is partly unresolved and I have not verified it independently.
Bohm is not available as a laureate.
The prize traditions are weaker for conceptual contributions without a single decisive experiment.
